summary: In Greek mythology, Chalciope (Ancient Greek: Χαλκιόπη, "bronze-face" or "with the brass voice") was a Colchian princess, daughter of King Aeëtes and the Oceanid Idyia, sister of Medea and Absyrtus. Aeëtes gave her in marriage without bride-gifts to Phrixus when he arrived on the golden ram; by him she bore Argus, Melas, Phrontis, and Cytisorus. In Apollonius she persuades Medea to aid Jason so that her sons — wrecked and rescued by the Argonauts — may survive. This atlas entry is the Colchian princess — not Aegeus's Athenian wife or other homonyms.

etymology: Ancient Greek Khalkiópē (Χαλκιόπη), literally "bronze-face" or "with the brass voice." Acusilaus, Hesiod, and Hesychius call her Iophossa; Pherecydes names her Euenia.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Chalciope's mother was the Oceanid Idyia; her siblings were Medea and Absyrtus. She married Phrixus and bore sons variously listed as Argus, Phrontis, Melas, and Cytisorus (with alternate name-lists in Hyginus and others; some add Presbon).

In Apollonius's Argonautica her son Argus tells Jason that Aeëtes received Phrixus gladly and gave him Chalciope without gifts of wooing; Phrixus died an aged man in Aeëtes's house, and the sons set out for Orchomenus to claim Athamas's possessions.

sections.heading: Medea and the Argonauts
paragraphs: When her sons were shipwrecked and rescued by the Argonauts, Chalciope rejoiced to find them among Jason's company and pleaded with Medea to help Jason — fearing Aeëtes's wrath against the boys if the quest failed. Their reunion and her tears are a turning point in Apollonius Book 3.

A later tradition (Hyginus) has her stay loyally with Aeëtes after Perses dethroned him, even though the king had killed Phrixus out of fear of an Aeolid oracle — a version at odds with Apollonius's peaceful old age for Phrixus.

sections.heading: Homonyms
paragraphs: Other women named Chalciope include the daughter of Rhexenor (or of Chalcodon), second wife of Aegeus of Athens who bore him no heirs; a Coan mother of Thessalus by Heracles; and the mother of Linus by Apollo. This notice concerns only Aeëtes's Colchian daughter.
